Chapter Seven: The New Tribalism—Fragmentation in a Connected Age
Isn’t it strange? We live in a world where everyone’s supposed to be more connected than ever, yet so many people feel alone.
Think about social media for a second—it promises to bring us together, but more often it sorts us into smaller and smaller groups.
Online, it’s almost effortless to find folks who think just like you, who share your fears, and see the world through the same lens.
And while that can feel comforting, it’s also the root of a new kind of tribalism—one that’s not tied to where we live, but to what we believe, or how we see ourselves.
Picture a teenager who doesn’t quite fit in at school. She finds her tribe online, a group that shares her interests. At first, it’s a relief—a place where she finally feels at home.
But over time, that group turns into an echo chamber. The same ideas get repeated, anything different is quietly pushed out, and suddenly, the world beyond their circle starts to seem threatening—or even dangerous.
This isn’t just one story. It’s happening everywhere. People are gathering around identities—political, religious, cultural, even little things like hobbies.
The lines between groups might be invisible, but they’re real. And once those boundaries are drawn, it’s easy to see outsiders as people who just “don’t get it.”
Real conversations get replaced by slogans. Curiosity slowly turns into suspicion.
Here’s the thing: Most people aren’t trying to build walls. They just want to feel safe, to feel heard and respected.
But the very tools of our digital age make it so easy to slip into bubbles—places where anything different feels scary, instead of interesting.
The big promise of connection? Sometimes it ends up as deep fragmentation.
And this new tribalism isn’t always loud or dramatic. Sometimes, it’s just quiet withdrawal—a choice to stop listening, to stop caring about what’s happening outside your group.
But even that has a big impact. The public square, already fragile in the face of global pressures, becomes even weaker.
The space where we could all talk and learn from each other? It gets smaller and smaller.
So, what’s the real challenge here? It’s not just about connecting more, but about connecting across our differences.
We need to build communities that are open, not closed—curious, not defensive.
Until we do, the world stays a patchwork of tribes, each convinced they’re right, and each missing out on the chance to learn something new from someone else.
